summary: Describes Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, derived largely from the IPv4 version in RFC 1191. It lets a sender learn the largest packet that can cross a path without being broken up. It was replaced by RFC 8201.

plainLanguage.summary: Every link in a network has a limit on the size of a packet it can carry, and the smallest limit along the path is what a sender must respect. This RFC describes how the sender finds that number: routers report it with a Packet Too Big message, and the sender tries again with smaller packets.

subtitle: How a sender learns the largest packet that can cross a path, using ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages.

tldr.problem: A sender does not know how large a packet can be before it reaches the destination, because the smallest link along the path may be much smaller than the sender's own link.
tldr.mechanism: The sender starts with the MTU of its first hop and sends packets. When a router cannot forward a packet because it is too large, the router discards it and returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message carrying the MTU of the constricting link, and the sender lowers its estimate and tries again.

sections.title: Why a Sender Needs to Know the Path MTU
sections.content:
When one IPv6 node has a large amount of data to send to another, the data is transmitted in a series of IPv6 packets. It is usually preferable for these packets to be of the largest size that can successfully traverse the path from source to destination. That size is the Path MTU, and it is equal to the minimum link MTU of all the links in the path. IPv6 defines a standard mechanism for a node to discover the PMTU of an arbitrary path.

IPv6 nodes SHOULD implement Path MTU Discovery, so that they can find and take advantage of paths whose PMTU is greater than the IPv6 minimum link MTU. A minimal IPv6 implementation, for example one in a boot ROM, may choose to omit it. Nodes that do not implement it use the IPv6 minimum link MTU as the maximum packet size. In most cases this results in packets that are smaller than necessary, because most paths have a PMTU greater than the IPv6 minimum link MTU. A node sending packets much smaller than the path allows is wasting network resources and probably getting suboptimal throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Each link in a network can only carry packets up to a certain size. The sender does not know that size in advance, because it depends on every router in between. Without Path MTU Discovery the sender has to guess small and lose speed.

sections.title: The Terms the RFC Uses
sections.content:
A node is a device that implements IPv6. A router is a node that forwards IPv6 packets not explicitly addressed to itself, and a host is any node that is not a router. An upper layer is a protocol layer immediately above IPv6, such as a transport protocol like TCP or UDP, a control protocol like ICMP, a routing protocol like OSPF, or an internet or lower-layer protocol tunneled over IPv6. A link is a communication facility over which nodes communicate at the link layer, and an interface is a node's attachment to a link.

A link MTU is the maximum transmission unit, that is the maximum packet size in octets, that can be conveyed in one piece over a link. A path is the set of links traversed by a packet between a source node and a destination node, and the path MTU is the minimum link MTU of all the links in that path. Path MTU Discovery is the process by which a node learns the PMTU of a path.

A flow is a sequence of packets sent from a particular source to a particular unicast or multicast destination for which the source desires special handling by the intervening routers, and a flow id is a combination of a source address and a non-zero flow label.
sections.plainLanguage: The link MTU is the biggest packet one link can carry. The path MTU is the smallest of those numbers across the whole path, so it is the size that limits what the sender can send.

sections.title: How the Discovery Loop Works
sections.content:
The basic idea is that a source node initially assumes that the PMTU of a path is the known MTU of the first hop in the path. If any of the packets sent on that path are too large to be forwarded by some node along it, that node discards them and returns ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages. On receiving such a message, the source node reduces its assumed PMTU for the path based on the MTU of the constraining hop as reported in the message.

The Path MTU Discovery process ends when the node's estimate of the PMTU is less than or equal to the actual PMTU. Several iterations of the packet-sent and Packet-Too-Big-message-received cycle may occur before it ends, because there may be links with smaller MTUs further along the path. A node may also elect to end the process by ceasing to send packets larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

The PMTU of a path may change over time as the routing topology changes. Reductions are detected by Packet Too Big messages. To detect increases, a node periodically raises its assumed PMTU, which almost always results in packets being discarded and Packet Too Big messages being generated, because in most cases the PMTU of the path has not changed. Attempts to detect increases should therefore be made infrequently.

Path MTU Discovery supports multicast as well as unicast destinations. With a multicast destination, copies of a packet may traverse many different paths, each with a different PMTU, so a single multicast packet may result in multiple Packet Too Big messages, each reporting a different next-hop MTU. The minimum PMTU across the set of paths in use determines the size of subsequent packets sent to that destination. The RFC also notes that Path MTU Discovery must be performed even when a node thinks a destination is attached to the same link as itself, because a neighboring router may act as a proxy for a destination that is in fact more than one hop away.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender starts with the size of its own link and sends a packet. If a router further along cannot forward it, that router drops it and sends back a message saying how big a packet would fit. The sender lowers its guess and tries again, repeating until the packets get through.

sections.title: What an Implementation Must Do
sections.content:
The requirements apply only to implementations that include Path MTU Discovery. When a node receives a Packet Too Big message it MUST reduce its estimate of the PMTU for the relevant path, based on the value of the MTU field in the message. The precise behaviour is not specified, since different applications have different requirements and different implementation architectures favour different strategies.

After receiving a Packet Too Big message, a node MUST attempt to avoid eliciting more such messages in the near future, by reducing the size of the packets it sends along the path. Using an estimate larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU may continue to elicit Packet Too Big messages, and since each message and the dropped packets it responds to consume network resources, the node MUST force the Path MTU Discovery process to end.

Nodes using Path MTU Discovery MUST detect decreases in PMTU as fast as possible. They MAY detect increases, but because doing so requires sending packets larger than the current estimate, and because the likelihood is that the PMTU has not increased, this MUST be done at infrequent intervals. An attempt to detect an increase MUST NOT be made less than 5 minutes after a Packet Too Big message has been received for the given path, and the recommended setting for this timer is twice its minimum value, 10 minutes. A node MUST NOT reduce its estimate of the Path MTU below the IPv6 minimum link MTU. If a Packet Too Big message reports a next-hop MTU below that minimum, the node is not required to send smaller packets, but must instead include a Fragment header in those packets.

A node MUST NOT increase its estimate of the Path MTU in response to the contents of a Packet Too Big message. A message announcing an increase might be a stale packet floating around the network, a false packet injected as part of a denial-of-service attack, or the result of having several paths to the destination with different PMTUs.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender must lower its estimate when it hears a Packet Too Big message, and it must stop sending oversized packets soon afterwards. It may try to find a bigger path again, but not more often than once every five minutes, and it must never believe a message that claims the path got bigger.

sections.title: Where the Information Is Kept and How It Ages
sections.content:
Section 5 is a set of notes for implementors rather than a specification. It suggests that the IP layer store the PMTU information and that the ICMP layer process the received Packet Too Big messages, with the packetization layers responding by changing the size of the messages they send. Packetization layers then need a way to learn of changes in MMS_S, the maximum send transport-message size, which is the Path MTU minus the size of the IPv6 header plus space reserved by the IP layer for additional headers.

A node will usually not have enough information to identify a path exactly, so it must associate a PMTU value with some local representation of a path. Minimally it could keep one PMTU for all packets, which would be the minimum learned across all paths and would often be smaller than necessary. Using the destination address as the local representation is better, and fits the model of a host with a destination cache. Using the flow id gives a per-flow value, which is finer still. Source route information can qualify the representation further.

Because routes change over time, cached PMTU information can become stale. A stale value that is too large is discovered as soon as a large enough packet is sent, but there is no mechanism for noticing that a stale value is too small, so cached values should be aged. When a PMTU value has not been decreased for a while, on the order of 10 minutes, the estimate should be set back to the MTU of the first-hop link and the packetization layers notified, which makes the whole discovery process run again. One implementation puts a timestamp on each cached PMTU value and runs a timer-driven procedure once a minute over all cached values, resetting any whose timestamp is older than the timeout interval. An implementation should provide a means for changing the timeout duration, including setting it to infinity, so that a node which will never discover a new non-local PMTU is not made to suffer dropped packets every 10 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC suggests the IP layer keep the size it learned, and the layer above react when it shrinks. Because routes change, an old size can be wrong in either direction, so cached values are reset to the first hop size every ten minutes or so to make the sender check again.

sections.title: Two Denial-of-Service Attacks
sections.content:
This Path MTU Discovery mechanism makes possible two denial-of-service attacks, both based on a malicious party sending false Packet Too Big messages to a node.

In the first attack the false message indicates a PMTU much smaller than reality. This should not entirely stop the flow of data, because the victim node should never set its PMTU estimate below the IPv6 minimum link MTU. It will, however, result in suboptimal performance.

In the second attack the false message indicates a PMTU larger than reality. If believed, this could cause temporary blockage, as the victim sends packets that some router will drop. Within one round-trip time the node would discover its mistake, because it would receive Packet Too Big messages from that router, but frequent repetition of the attack could cause a lot of packets to be dropped. A node, however, should never raise its estimate of the PMTU based on a Packet Too Big message, so it should not be vulnerable to this attack. A malicious party could also cause problems by stopping a victim from receiving legitimate Packet Too Big messages, but the RFC notes that simpler denial-of-service attacks are available for that.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can send false Packet Too Big messages can slow a sender down. Announcing a path that is too small hurts performance; announcing one that is too large is harmless, because the sender never believes a message that claims the path grew.
